14 / The learning salon

Women in computing history

From symbolic instructions to flight software. Four pioneers whose work helped change what computers could do.

{ }

Computing history was not made by one genius at a lonely desk. It is also a story of teams, collaboration and women whose work deserves attention.

The connections to Ada below are thematic parallels. We do not claim that she directly inspired or personally influenced each of these scientists.

GH
A-0 · FLOW-MATIC

Grace Hopper

Grace Hopper developed early compilers and FLOW-MATIC, a language that influenced COBOL. She helped bring programming closer to human language. COBOL was a collaboration between multiple people and organisations.

How this story connects to Ada

Understandable symbols can represent precise instructions. The bridge between human intention and what a machine can execute matters.

Computer History Museum: Grace Hopper ↗
MH
Apollo

Margaret Hamilton

Margaret Hamilton led the team developing flight software for the Apollo programme. Her work included reliability, testing and task priorities. Successful missions depended on many specialists working together.

How this story connects to Ada

An idea for a calculation is not enough. We need a precise procedure and must consider what happens under unexpected conditions.

NASA: Margaret Hamilton ↗
JB
ENIAC

Jean Bartik

Jean Bartik was one of the six original ENIAC programmers. She later helped convert it into a stored-program computer and also worked on BINAC and UNIVAC I.

How this story connects to Ada

A mathematical problem must be broken into operations a machine can handle. Programming involves more than typing into an editor.

Computer History Museum: Jean Bartik ↗
FA
IBM · PTRAN

Frances Allen

Frances Allen researched compiler optimisation and automatic parallel execution. Her work helped programs run more efficiently. She became the first woman to receive the Turing Award, for 2006.

How this story connects to Ada

The order and organisation of calculations affect performance. Good programming also means finding a more effective procedure.

IBM: Frances Allen ↗
